alalal-c51086-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 27: whether numerically one wisdom can exist in the minds of different people.

alalal-c51086-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's (Augustine's) comparison of wisdom in two wise men of unequal size: some infer from it that numerically one wisdom is in different minds, and their arguments are to be set out.

alalal-c51086-d1e143.summary: First argument for numerical unity: if wisdom were one only in species, Augustine's example would fail, since God, numerically one, is in all places.

alalal-c51086-d1e154.summary: Second argument: if two wisdoms were numerically distinct, they would be more than one, contrary to Augustine's saying that two wisdoms are not more than one.

alalal-c51086-d1e176.summary: Third argument: 'man is an animal', known by many, is either the same truth in all minds, or there is a truth common to them all, making the proposition common rather than singular, which is false.

alalal-c51086-d1e200.summary: Fourth argument: 'man' understood by different people is either the same concept, so complex truths are also the same, or 'man' would be common to these concepts and thus a subaltern genus rather than a most specific species.

alalal-c51086-d1e226.summary: Fifth argument: the more powerful the agent, the more like itself its effect; if a form in matter can generate its like, a form in the nobler intellect would generate something numerically identical, so that if I could see your thoughts they would generate themselves numerically in my mind.

alalal-c51086-d1e252.summary: Sixth argument: intellect and intellect agree more than matter and intellect; if one form can be numerically the same in matter and intellect, all the more in two intellects.

alalal-c51086-d1e269.summary: Seventh argument: otherwise each angel would know only the truths in its own mind and be ignorant of far more truths in the minds of others, which is unfitting.

alalal-c51086-d1e287.summary: Transitional remark: these are their arguments, and further arguments can be offered on their behalf.

alalal-c51086-d1e294.summary: Eighth argument from Metaphysics VII: if forms were separate from things, as Plato held, nothing would be known through them; so the form in the soul must be the same as the form in the thing, and since forms identical with one thing are identical with each other, the species in all souls are the same, and so is knowledge.
concepts: identity of form in thing and soul

alalal-c51086-d1e332.summary: Ninth argument: in immaterial things intellect and understood are identical, and speculative knowledge is identical with what is known; the Commentator extends this to every intelligible, so the species in the soul is identical with the species in matter, and speculative knowledge is numerically one in all minds.

alalal-c51086-d1e367.summary: Tenth argument from De anima III: the intellect in act is the thing understood, from which the same conclusion follows.
concepts: intellect in act is the intelligible

alalal-c51086-d1e378.summary: Eleventh argument: a potency reduced to act has the numerically same act it was in potency to; the intellect is in potency to the species of things (De anima III: intellect is the form of forms, as the hand is the tool of tools), so the same numerical form is in intellect and matter, and all knowledge is numerically one.

alalal-c51086-d1e451.summary: Twelfth argument, from the Commentator: what is separated from here and now and other individuating conditions is the same for all, always and everywhere; every intelligible is so separated, so the speculative intellect is the same in all souls.

alalal-c51086-d1e475.summary: Notes that these added arguments seem stronger than the first set.

alalal-c51086-d1e484.summary: Contrary argument: knowledge is an act, quality and habit denominating the soul (Aristotle, Augustine), and one accident cannot be in different subjects, so one knowledge cannot be in different souls.

alalal-c51086-d1e510.summary: Second contrary argument: the same numerical truth would then be both known and forgotten.

alalal-c51086-d1e521.summary: Third, stronger argument: if the substantial form in the thing is the same as in the soul, it is in the soul either as in matter, so that the intellect would receive being and nature from the form of a donkey or goat, or in some other way; but every form needs a subject as matter, so the donkey would be in the soul by matter and form, which Aristotle denies.
concepts: mode of form's presence in intellect

alalal-c51086-d1e573.summary: Fourth: nothing receives simultaneously several acts differing in species or genus, yet the intellect receives all forms at once, so it does not receive them as the same substantial forms that are in things.

alalal-c51086-d1e592.summary: Fifth: every form inheres, and if the same form were in the soul, it would give the soul being and nature by itself, so an intellect understanding a donkey would be a donkey, which is ridiculous.

alalal-c51086-d1e618.summary: Sixth: all philosophers, Avicenna, Algazel, Aristotle and Augustine, place knowledge in the category of quality.

alalal-c51086-d1e634.summary: Solution: the species in the soul are not numerically the same as the forms of external things, and one person's knowledge is not the same as another's. A species can be considered in relation to the soul, as an accident and passion existing in it, or as the intention of a thing; as intention it is one for all, since the thing is one, but numbered by those who intend the thing through it, there are as many as there are knowers.
claims: Mental species are not numerically identical with external forms or across knowers.
A species is one as the intention of one thing, but many as accidents in many minds.

alalal-c51086-d1e678.summary: Reply to the first argument: Augustine's example holds of the intention constituting knowledge as numbered from the thing, since in that way it makes the thing known.

alalal-c51086-d1e691.summary: Reply to the second argument: in the same way, two knowledges will be the same.

alalal-c51086-d1e700.summary: Reply to the third and fourth arguments: a dictum is singular not because its species is one in the soul but because of the one intention of the thing in this and that soul; Socrates' individuality is not one in everyone's senses yet is singular by the thing it determines. The intention 'man' receives nothing added in different souls, so it is not made common to them and remains singular.
claims: Concepts are not made common genera by existing in many minds, since nothing is added to them there.

alalal-c51086-d1e745.summary: Reply to the fifth and sixth arguments: they proceed from falsehoods, since the Philosopher says a form in matter generates a form like itself in species, not the same in number; nor is the same numerical species in soul and in matter.

alalal-c51086-d1e776.summary: Reply to the Aristotelian arguments: intellect in act and the thing understood are the same in that both are actualised by one act, the species of the thing, which gives being in the thing and is a separated intention in the intellect; so they are the same act but not the same in being or number. Others restrict the identity to separate intellects like angels, but that is false and not Aristotle's meaning.
claims: Intellect in act and intelligible in act share one act, the species, which exists differently in thing and mind, so they are not numerically identical.

alalal-c51086-d1e837.summary: Reply to the Commentator: he takes the intention as related to the thing whose ratio it is, and in this sense it is numbered by the thing, not by those who intend through it.

alalal-c51086.summary: Article 27 asks whether numerically one wisdom can exist in different minds, as some read Augustine's analogy in Lombard's text. Twelve arguments, several drawing on Aristotle and Averroes, claim that it can: from the identity of intellect and intelligible, from the form in the soul being the same as the form in things, and from intelligibles being free of individuating conditions. Contrary arguments note that knowledge is a quality inhering in the soul and that the intellect cannot receive real substantial forms without becoming what it knows. Albert holds that species and knowledge are not numerically identical across minds or with external forms. A species is an accident in the soul, multiplied by knowers, and an intention of the thing, one by the unity of the thing. Intellect and intelligible are one in act because the same species gives being in the thing and is an intention in the mind, but they are not one in number. Concepts are not made common genera by existing in many minds.
claims: Knowledge is not numerically one in different minds.
A mental species is many as an accident in many souls but one as the intention of one thing.
Intellect and intelligible are one in act, not in number, since the species exists naturally in the thing and intentionally in the mind.
